Attention Is All You Need

A pure-attention encoder–decoder architecture—the Transformer—that eliminates sequence-aligned recurrence and convolution to achieve constant-depth global dependencies, massive parallelization, and state-of-the-art machine translation at a fraction of prior compute.

Core Overview

Vaswani et al. replace sequence-aligned recurrence and convolutions with stacked multi-head self-attention and point-wise feed-forward layers, decoupling sequence length from sequential computation depth.

  • Bottleneck broken: Recurrent networks compute hidden states $h_t$ sequentially from $h_{t-1}$, blocking within-example parallelization, while convolutional alternatives require stacks growing linearly ($O(n/k)$) or logarithmically ($O(\log_k n)$) with token distance.
  • Core mechanism: Scaled Dot-Product Attention divides inner products by $\sqrt{d_k}$ to avoid softmax gradient saturation, Multi-Head Attention projects queries, keys, and values into $h=8$ parallel subspaces to overcome averaging blur, and fixed sinusoidal encodings inject order with linear relative-shift structure.
  • Decisive translation leap: On WMT 2014 EN-DE, even the 12-hour base Transformer (27.3 BLEU, $3.3\times 10^{18}$ FLOPs) beats every prior published model and ensemble; the 3.5-day big model reaches 28.4 BLEU on EN-DE and 41.8 single-model BLEU on EN-FR ($2.3\times 10^{19}$ FLOPs).
  • Generalization beyond translation: Without task-specific architectural engineering, a 4-layer Transformer generalizes to English constituency parsing—where outputs obey strict syntactic constraints and exceed input length—outperforming BerkeleyParser even in the 40K-sentence WSJ-only regime.

01 Motivation & Sequence Transduction Background §1–§2

The Sequential Computation Bottleneck §1

Prior to this paper, recurrent neural networks—specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU)—were the established state of the art for sequence modeling and transduction tasks such as language modeling and machine translation. Recurrent architectures factor computation along symbol positions, generating hidden states $h_t$ as a function of the previous hidden state $h_{t-1}$ and the current input at position $t$.

That sequential dependency precludes parallelization within individual training examples. As sequence lengths grow, memory limits also constrain batching across examples, turning sequential recurrence into a hard training bottleneck. While factorization tricks and sparsely-gated conditional computation (MoE) improved efficiency and quality, neither removed the underlying sequential constraint. Attention mechanisms had already proven indispensable for modeling dependencies regardless of token distance, yet in nearly all systems they remained bolted onto a recurrent backbone.

Convolutional & Self-Attentive Predecessors §2

Several earlier architectures sought to eliminate recurrence by adopting convolutional building blocks that compute hidden representations for all positions in parallel—notably Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet, and ConvS2S. However, in convolutional networks, the number of operations required to connect two arbitrary positions grows with their distance: linearly ($O(n/k)$) in ConvS2S and logarithmically ($O(\log_k n)$) in dilated-convolution models like ByteNet, which impedes learning long-range dependencies. The Transformer reduces this connection distance to a constant $O(1)$ operations. Doing so introduces a trade-off—averaging attention-weighted positions reduces effective resolution—which the authors explicitly counteract with Multi-Head Attention.

Self-attention (also termed intra-attention), which relates different positions within a single sequence to build its representation, had previously succeeded in reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment, and sentence representation learning. End-to-end memory networks also relied on recurrent attention rather than sequence-aligned recurrence for simple question answering and language modeling. To the authors' knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute input and output representations without sequence-aligned RNNs or convolutions.

02 The Transformer Architecture §3

Encoder and Decoder Stacks §3.1

Following the standard neural sequence transduction formulation, the encoder maps an input symbol sequence $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ to a sequence of continuous representations $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, \dots, z_n)$. Given $\mathbf{z}$, the decoder generates an output sequence $(y_1, \dots, y_m)$ one symbol at a time; at each generation step the model is auto-regressive, consuming previously generated symbols as additional input when predicting the next.

Both stacks consist of $N = 6$ identical layers (Figure 1). Every sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection followed by layer normalization (a post-norm design), requiring all embeddings and sub-layer outputs to share dimension $d_{\text{model}} = 512$:

Residual Sub-Layer Formulation · §3.1
$$\mathrm{Output} = \mathrm{LayerNorm}\bigl(x + \mathrm{Sublayer}(x)\bigr)$$
During training (§5.4), residual dropout ($P_{\text{drop}} = 0.1$ in base) is applied to $\mathrm{Sublayer}(x)$ before it is added to $x$ and normalized.

Scaled Dot-Product Attention & The $\sqrt{d_k}$ Variance Proof §3.2.1

An attention function maps a query and a set of key–value pairs to an output vector computed as a weighted sum of values, where each weight comes from a compatibility score between the query and its key. Packing queries, keys, and values into matrices $Q$, $K$, and $V$ (with key/query dimension $d_k$ and value dimension $d_v$), the paper defines Scaled Dot-Product Attention as:

Eq. (1) · Scaled Dot-Product Attention · §3.2.1
$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V$$
Without the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ factor, this is standard multiplicative (dot-product) attention. Compared to additive attention (a single-hidden-layer FFN), both share theoretical complexity, but dot-product attention is far faster and more space-efficient in practice via optimized matrix multiplication (GEMM).

Why is the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling necessary? While additive and unscaled dot-product attention perform similarly for small $d_k$, additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention as $d_k$ grows. Footnote 4 of the paper provides the exact statistical argument: if the components of $q$ and $k$ are independent random variables with mean $0$ and variance $1$, their dot product $q \cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i$ has mean $0$ and variance $d_k$ (standard deviation $\sqrt{d_k}$). Large-magnitude logits push softmax into flat saturation regions where gradients vanish; dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance regardless of $d_k$.

Interactive Lab 1 · Why $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ Prevents Softmax Gradient Collapse (Eq. 1 & Footnote 4)
Footnote 4 Grounded

What to observe: Drag $d_k$ from $4$ to $512$. Unscaled $q\cdot k$ logits widen as $\sqrt{d_k}$, collapsing softmax onto a single peak (near-zero entropy and vanishing Jacobian $p(1-p)$), whereas dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ keeps the attention distribution and gradient magnitude invariant across every dimension.

Static summary of this effect across 2,000 i.i.d. $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ trials with 8 keys: at the base head size $d_k = 64$, unscaled dot products already have standard deviation $8.0$, pushing mean maximum attention weight to $0.875$ and cutting mean peak Jacobian $p(1-p)$ to $0.083$; at $d_k = 512$, peak weight hits $0.958$ and $p(1-p)$ plunges to $0.030$. Under $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling, max weight remains steady at $\approx 0.36$ and $p(1-p) \approx 0.216$ across all $d_k$.

Multi-Head Attention & Three Attention Roles §3.2.2–§3.2.3

Rather than executing one attention function on full $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional representations—where averaging suppresses distinct positional or syntactic signals—the Transformer linearly projects $Q$, $K$, and $V$ into $h$ learned subspaces of dimensions $d_k, d_k, d_v$, runs Scaled Dot-Product Attention in parallel on each head, concatenates the outputs, and projects back to $d_{\text{model}}$:

Multi-Head Attention · §3.2.2
$$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{MultiHead}(Q, K, V) &= \mathrm{Concat}(\mathrm{head}_1, \dots, \mathrm{head}_h)\, W^O \\ \text{where}\quad \mathrm{head}_i &= \mathrm{Attention}\bigl(Q W_i^Q,\, K W_i^K,\, V W_i^V\bigr) \end{aligned}$$
Projection matrices: $W_i^Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$, $W_i^K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_k}$, $W_i^V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_v}$, and $W^O \in \mathbb{R}^{h d_v \times d_{\text{model}}}$. With base settings $h = 8$ and $d_k = d_v = d_{\text{model}}/h = 64$, total computational cost matches single-head full-dimensional attention.

To ground these matrix operations concretely, Explainer B walks through a 3-token sequence (["The", "law", "applies"]) with $d_{\text{model}}=4$, $h=2$, and $d_k=d_v=2$, displaying the exact computed numbers at each stage—including how causal masking in decoder self-attention zeroes future weights without altering past normalization.

Across the full architecture, Multi-Head Attention serves three distinct structural roles (§3.2.3):

1 · Encoder Self-AttnBidirectional
$Q, K, V$ all originate from the previous encoder layer. Every source position attends freely to all source positions in one step.
2 · Decoder Self-AttnMasked ($-\infty$)
$Q, K, V$ come from the previous decoder layer, but entries corresponding to positions $> i$ are masked to $-\infty$ before softmax to preserve auto-regression.
3 · Cross-AttentionEnc → Dec
Queries $Q$ come from the previous decoder layer, while memory keys $K$ and values $V$ come from the top encoder output $\mathbf{z}$, letting every target position inspect the entire source sequence.

Position-wise Feed-Forward Networks, Weight-Tied Embeddings & Positional Encoding §3.3–§3.5

Every encoder and decoder layer pairs its attention sub-layer(s) with a Position-wise Feed-Forward Network applied identically and independently to each token position—equivalently, two convolutions of kernel size $1$:

Eq. (2) · Position-wise Feed-Forward Network · §3.3
$$\mathrm{FFN}(x) = \max(0,\, x W_1 + b_1)\, W_2 + b_2$$
Input and output dimensionality is $d_{\text{model}} = 512$, expanding to inner dimensionality $d_{\text{ff}} = 2048$ (4× expansion; $1024 \to 4096$ in big). Parameters are shared across sequence positions within a layer, but differ across layers.

Embeddings and Softmax (§3.4): Learned embeddings convert input and output tokens into $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional vectors, and a learned linear layer plus softmax maps decoder outputs to next-token probabilities. Following Press & Wolf [30], the Transformer shares a single weight matrix across the input embedding, output embedding, and pre-softmax linear projection, multiplying embedding weights by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$ ($\approx 22.63$ for base).

Sinusoidal Positional Encoding (§3.5): Because the architecture has neither recurrence nor convolution, it injects sequence order by summing fixed $d_{\text{model}}$-dimensional positional encodings directly onto input and output embeddings at the bottoms of both stacks:

Sinusoidal Positional Encoding · §3.5
$$PE_{(pos,\, 2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i / d_{\text{model}}}}\right), \qquad PE_{(pos,\, 2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i / d_{\text{model}}}}\right)$$
Here $pos$ is token position and $i$ is the dimension pair index ($0 \le i < d_{\text{model}}/2$). Wavelengths form a geometric progression from $2\pi$ to $10000 \cdot 2\pi$.

The authors hypothesize that sinusoidal encodings make learning relative-position attention easy because for any fixed offset $k$, $PE_{pos+k}$ is a linear function of $PE_{pos}$. Empirically, learned positional embeddings yield nearly identical dev performance (Table 3 row E: 25.7 vs. 25.8 BLEU), so the authors prefer sinusoids for their potential to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than those seen in training.

Proof Sketch · Why $PE_{pos+k}$ Is an Exact Linear Transformation of $PE_{pos}$ Math Derivation

Let $\omega_i = 10000^{-2i/d_{\text{model}}}$. For each sine/cosine pair $(2i,\, 2i+1)$, standard angle-addition identities yield an orthogonal $2\times 2$ rotation matrix $M_k^{(i)}$ that depends only on offset $k$, never on absolute position $pos$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} \sin\bigl(\omega_i(pos + k)\bigr) \\ \cos\bigl(\omega_i(pos + k)\bigr) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos(\omega_i k) & \sin(\omega_i k) \\ -\sin(\omega_i k) & \cos(\omega_i k) \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \sin(\omega_i\, pos) \\ \cos(\omega_i\, pos) \end{bmatrix}$$

Stacking $M_k^{(i)}$ across all $i = 0, \dots, d_{\text{model}}/2 - 1$ yields a block-diagonal linear operator $M_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{model}}\times d_{\text{model}}}$ satisfying $PE_{pos+k} = M_k\, PE_{pos}$. Furthermore, the inner product $PE_{pos} \cdot PE_{pos+k} = \sum_i \cos(\omega_i k)$ depends purely on relative distance $|k|$.

03 Why Self-Attention: Complexity, Parallelism & Interpretability §4

To motivate replacing recurrence and convolutions with self-attention for mapping a sequence $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ to $(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ ($x_i, z_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$), Section 4 evaluates layer types on three desiderata: (1) total computational complexity per layer, (2) parallelizability measured by minimum sequential operations, and (3) maximum path length between long-range dependencies—shorter forward and backward signal paths make distant dependencies easier to learn.

Layer Type Complexity per Layer Sequential Operations Maximum Path Length
Self-Attention $O(n^2 \cdot d)$ $O(1)$ $O(1)$
Recurrent $O(n \cdot d^2)$ $O(n)$ $O(n)$
Convolutional $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$ $O(1)$ $O(\log_k(n))$
Self-Attention (restricted) $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$ $O(1)$ $O(n/r)$
Note on Table 1: $n$ is sequence length, $d$ is representation dimension, $k$ is convolutional kernel width, and $r$ is neighborhood size in restricted self-attention. The $O(\log_k(n))$ path length for convolutions assumes dilated convolutions [18]; contiguous kernels require $O(n/k)$ layers.

Three regime insights follow directly from Table 1:

  • Fast when $n < d$: Self-attention requires fewer total operations per layer than a recurrent layer whenever sequence length $n$ is smaller than representation dimension $d$—the typical regime for subword-tokenized machine translation sentences (where $n \approx 20$–$100$ and $d = 512$).
  • Long-sequence restriction trade-off: For very long sequences ($n \gg d$), restricting self-attention to a centered neighborhood of size $r$ lowers complexity to $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$ at the expense of raising maximum path length to $O(n/r)$ (noted by the authors as future work, not benchmarked in this paper).
  • Comparison with convolutions: Standard convolutions cost $k\times$ more than recurrent layers ($O(k\cdot n\cdot d^2)$). Depthwise separable convolutions lower this to $O(k\cdot n\cdot d + n\cdot d^2)$; remarkably, even at full width $k = n$, separable convolution complexity equals the exact combination of a self-attention layer ($O(n^2 d)$) and a point-wise FFN ($O(n d^2)$)—the Transformer's building block.

Interpretability & Attention Visualizations §4 · Appendix (pp. 13–15)

As a side benefit, self-attention exposes interpretable token-to-token routing patterns. Inspecting attention distributions in encoder layer 5 of 6 reveals that individual heads specialize in distinct linguistic tasks, including long-distance predicate completion, anaphora resolution, and syntactic phrase structure. All three appendix visualization plates (Figures 3–5) are preserved below at high resolution.

Appendix · Attention Visualizations (Original Figures 3, 4 & 5, pp. 13–15) Appendix

Long-distance dependency completion (Figure 3): In encoder self-attention layer 5 of 6, multiple attention heads (shown in distinct colors) from the verb "making" skip across five intervening tokens ("the registration or voting process") to attend sharply onto "more difficult", completing the discontinuous verb phrase "making… more difficult".

Anaphora resolution (Figure 4): Also in encoder layer 5 of 6, heads 5 and 6 exhibit razor-sharp attention from the possessive pronoun "its" directly back to its antecedent "Law" and head noun "application" in the sentence "The Law will never be perfect, but its application should be just…".

Specialized structural heads (Figure 5): Two additional heads from encoder layer 5 of 6 illustrate how different heads learn complementary structural roles on the exact same sentence—one linking clause-level heads and predicates (top, green), another tracking tight local/syntactic phrase relations (bottom, red).

04 Training Regime & Optimization §5

Datasets, Tokenization, Batching & Hardware §5.1–§5.2

The models are trained on two standard WMT 2014 translation benchmarks on a single machine equipped with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs:

  • WMT 2014 English–German: ~4.5 million sentence pairs encoded with Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) using a shared source–target vocabulary of ~37,000 tokens.
  • WMT 2014 English–French: 36 million sentence pairs split into a 32,000-token word-piece vocabulary.
  • Length-bucketed batching: Sentence pairs are grouped by approximate sequence length so each training batch contains roughly 25,000 source tokens and 25,000 target tokens.
  • Training schedule: Base models run at ~0.4 s/step for 100,000 steps (~12 hours). Big models run at 1.0 s/step for 300,000 steps (3.5 days).

Adam Optimizer & Noam Learning Rate Schedule §5.3

Optimization uses Adam with $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.98$, and $\epsilon = 10^{-9}$, paired with a custom linear-warmup / inverse-square-root decay learning rate schedule ($\text{warmup\_steps} = 4000$):

Eq. (3) · Warmup & Inverse-Square-Root Learning Rate Schedule · §5.3
$$\mathrm{lrate} = d_{\text{model}}^{-0.5} \cdot \min\!\left(\text{step\_num}^{-0.5},\; \text{step\_num} \cdot \text{warmup\_steps}^{-1.5}\right)$$
For $\text{step\_num} \le \text{warmup\_steps}$, the learning rate rises linearly from near zero to its peak $(d_{\text{model}}\cdot\text{warmup\_steps})^{-0.5}$ ($6.99\times 10^{-4}$ for base $d_{\text{model}}=512$; $4.94\times 10^{-4}$ for big $d_{\text{model}}=1024$), then decays as $\text{step\_num}^{-0.5}$.

Regularization §5.4

The paper describes two named regularization mechanisms during training: Residual Dropout applies dropout ($P_{\text{drop}} = 0.1$ for base; $0.3$ for EN-DE big, $0.1$ for EN-FR big) to the output of each sub-layer before residual addition and normalization, as well as to the sums of embeddings and positional encodings in both stacks. Label Smoothing ($\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$) distributes probability mass away from hard one-hot targets; as noted in §5.4 and confirmed in Table 3 row D, this deliberately worsens perplexity (4.92 vs. 4.67 at $\epsilon_{ls}=0$) because the model becomes less overconfident, yet improves downstream accuracy and BLEU (+0.5 BLEU on dev).

Edition note on §5.4: Page 7 introduces §5.4 with the sentence "We employ three types of regularization during training:", yet page 8 lists only two subsections (Residual Dropout and Label Smoothing). Section 6.3 (p. 9) briefly mentions tuning "dropout, both attention and residual (section 5.4)", suggesting attention dropout was likely the third item trimmed from an earlier draft.

05 Empirical Results: Translation, Ablations & Parsing §6

Machine Translation & Training-Compute Pareto Frontier §6.1

For evaluation on WMT 2014 newstest2014, the authors form a single model by averaging the last 5 checkpoints (written every 10 minutes) for base models and the last 20 checkpoints for big models. Inference uses beam search with beam size $4$, length penalty $\alpha = 0.6$, and maximum output length set to $\text{input length} + 50$ with early termination.

Notice that doubling $d_{\text{ff}}$ to 4096 (+25M params, +0.4 BLEU) yields twice the BLEU gain of doubling $d_{\text{model}}$ to 1024 (+103M params, +0.2 BLEU) at fixed 100K steps.

Synthesizing Table 3 into engineering roles clarifies which pieces of the Transformer are load-bearing and which remain open or interchangeable:

Architectural Component Role Verdict Exact Table 3 Evidence & Mechanism
Multi-Head Subspaces ($h = 8$–$16$) Indispensable Core Row (A): collapsing to $h=1$ loses $-0.9$ BLEU (+0.37 PPL); pushing to $h=32$ ($d_k=16$) also drops $-0.4$ BLEU.
Key Dimensionality ($d_k \ge 32$–$64$) Indispensable Core Row (B): shrinking $d_k$ to 32 or 16 drops $-0.4$ / $-0.7$ BLEU, indicating dot-product compatibility needs sufficient subspace capacity.
Residual Dropout ($P_{\text{drop}} \approx 0.1$) Indispensable Core Row (D): removing dropout ($0.0$) spikes PPL by $+0.85$ and drops $-1.2$ BLEU due to overfitting.
Label Smoothing ($\epsilon_{ls} = 0.1$) Conditional Gain Row (D): $\epsilon_{ls}=0$ achieves better PPL (4.67 vs. 4.92) yet loses $-0.5$ BLEU; trades calibration sharpness for translation quality.
FFN Width ($d_{\text{ff}}$) vs. Depth ($N$) Boundary Choice Row (C): $N=2$ collapses ($-2.1$ BLEU), $N=8$ slightly trails $N=6$ on dev BLEU ($-0.3$ despite better PPL 4.88), while $d_{\text{ff}}=4096$ adds $+0.4$ BLEU.
Sinusoidal vs. Learned PE Equivalent on Dev Row (E): learned embeddings match PPL exactly (4.92) and differ by only $-0.1$ BLEU; sinusoids chosen for hypothesized extrapolation.
$1/\sqrt{d_k}$ Scaling, Post-Norm, Weight Tying Unablated in Table 3 Justified theoretically (Footnote 4) or from prior literature [30], but never toggled off in Table 3 controls.

Generalization to English Constituency Parsing §6.3

To test whether the Transformer transfers beyond machine translation, Section 6.3 evaluates English constituency parsing—a demanding benchmark where outputs are linearized parse trees obeying strict structural constraints and running significantly longer than inputs, and where earlier RNN seq2seq models struggled in small-data regimes.

The authors train a 4-layer Transformer ($d_{\text{model}} = 1024$) in two settings: (1) WSJ-only (~40K Penn Treebank training sentences, 16K vocabulary) and (2) semi-supervised (~17M sentences combining high-confidence and BerkeleyParser corpora, 32K vocabulary). Only minimal tuning of dropout, learning rate, and beam size was performed on WSJ Section 22; all other hyperparameters remained identical to the EN-DE base translation model. Inference used beam size $21$, length penalty $\alpha = 0.3$, and maximum output length $\text{input length} + 300$.

Without task-specific architecture changes, the 4-layer Transformer outperforms all previously reported discriminative and semi-supervised parsers except the Recurrent Neural Network Grammar (RNNG [8], which achieves 91.7 WSJ-only and 93.3 generative) and multi-task Luong et al. (93.0). Crucially, unlike RNN seq2seq parsers (88.3 F1 on WSJ-only), the Transformer surpasses BerkeleyParser (90.4 F1) by $+0.9$ F1 even with only 40K training sentences.

06 Conclusion, Limitations & Architectural Implications §7

Authors' Conclusion & Future Agenda §7

Vaswani et al. conclude that the Transformer—the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention—trains substantially faster than recurrent or convolutional architectures while setting new state-of-the-art benchmarks on both WMT 2014 EN-DE (surpassing all prior ensembles) and WMT 2014 EN-FR translation. Looking forward, the authors highlight three open research directions: extending attention-based models beyond text to images, audio, and video; developing local, restricted attention mechanisms to handle large inputs and outputs efficiently; and making sequence generation itself less sequential. Full training and evaluation code was released in tensorflow/tensor2tensor.

Limitations & Scope Boundaries

1 · Quadratic Sequence Scaling ($O(n^2 d)$)

Full self-attention beats RNN per-layer complexity only when $n < d$ (Table 1). Although §4 proposes restricted neighborhood self-attention ($O(r n d)$) for very long inputs, it is never implemented or evaluated in this work.

2 · Sequential Auto-Regressive Inference

While encoder layers and teacher-forced decoder training parallelize across all positions in $O(1)$ sequential steps, test-time decoding remains strictly auto-regressive—generating $(y_1,\dots,y_m)$ one token per step (§3, explicitly flagged as future work in §7).

3 · Hardware-Estimated FLOPs & Unreported Memory

Table 2 FLOPs are estimated from wall-clock time $\times$ GPUs $\times$ sustained peak TFLOPS (Footnote 5) rather than exact operation counts, and the $O(n^2)$ attention-matrix activation memory footprint is not quantitatively reported.

4 · Unablated Components & Minor v7 Artifacts

Table 3 does not ablate $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling, LayerNorm placement, weight tying, or actual out-of-length sinusoidal extrapolation. Edition v7 also retains two minor textual inconsistencies: §6.1 prose states 41.0 EN-FR BLEU where Abstract and Table 2 report 41.8, and §5.4 announces three regularizers while listing two.

Engineering & Adoption Implications

01 · HEAD CAPACITY FLOOR

Balance $h$ Against Per-Head $d_k$

Table 3(A–B) shows a clear U-shaped trade-off: too few heads ($h=1$) lose subspace specialization, while shrinking $d_k$ below 32 starves dot-product compatibility. Keep $d_k \ge 32$–$64$ when choosing head counts.

02 · CAPACITY ALLOCATION

Prefer FFN Width Over Blind Depth

Under a fixed 100K-step budget (Table 3C), widening $d_{\text{ff}}$ from 2048 to 4096 adds $+0.4$ BLEU for only $+25\text{M}$ parameters, outperforming both deeper stacks ($N=8$, $-0.3$ BLEU) and wider residual streams ($d_{\text{model}}=1024$, $+0.2$ BLEU for $+103\text{M}$ params).

03 · METRIC DECOUPLING

Do Not Tune $\epsilon_{ls}$ by Perplexity Alone

Label smoothing ($\epsilon_{ls}=0.1$) degrades validation perplexity by $+0.25$ yet raises BLEU by $+0.5$ (Table 3D). Always validate regularization choices directly on the target task metric rather than cross-entropy alone.
